standard_text: Apply the properties of operations (i.e., identity, inverse, commutative, associative, distributive properties) to create equivalent linear expressions and to justify whether two linear expressions are equivalent when the two expressions name the same number regardless of which value is substituted into them. (E)

progression.narrative: 6.NS.7 asks students to do two things with linear expressions: CREATE equivalent ones (using the properties of operations) and JUSTIFY equivalence (by substitution). The logic runs from naming to rearranging to transforming to proving. First a student has to see an expression as parts -- variable, coefficient, constant, term (S1) -- because every property statement is about what happens to those parts. Then comes the first real act of creating an equivalent expression: combining like terms (S2), where 6r + 6 + r + 2 + 2r becomes 9r + 8 and the student learns that only terms counting the same thing can merge. The commutative and associative properties (S3) explain WHY that rearranging is legal -- and where it isn't: order can be swapped for addition and multiplication, never for subtraction or division. The distributive property (S4) is the standard's centerpiece transformation: 3(2x + 5) = 6x + 15 in both directions, expanding and factoring, with the multiplier reaching BOTH terms inside the parentheses. Substitution (S5) is the standard's own test of truth: two expressions are equivalent only if they name the same number for EVERY value of the variable, so plugging in a value settles any equivalence dispute. Finally the properties combine (S6): distribute, then rearrange, then combine like terms to simplify expressions like 2(3x + 4) + 5x + 1 and to write several different names for the same expression -- the full 'create and justify' demand of the standard.

steps.rationale: Name the parts. Every property is a statement about what may move or merge, so students must first see 5x + 8 as a coefficient, a variable, and a constant -- separate terms, not one blob of symbols.
The first way to create an equivalent expression: merge like terms. 6r + 6 + r + 2 + 2r and 9r + 8 name the same number, and only terms that count the same thing can be combined.

The commutative and associative properties are the license behind rearranging and regrouping -- and they only cover addition and multiplication. Knowing where the license STOPS (subtraction, division) is half the skill.

The distributive property is the standard's central transformation: 3(2x + 5) = 6x + 15, in both directions (expanding and factoring with the GCF). The multiplier must reach both terms in the parentheses.

The standard's own definition of equivalent: the two expressions name the same number for EVERY value substituted in. Substitution turns 'are these equivalent?' from a guess about appearance into a checkable fact.
The full demand: chain the properties together -- distribute, rearrange, combine like terms -- to simplify multi-step expressions and to write several different equivalent forms of one expression.

skills.name: Identify variables, coefficients, constants, and terms in expressions
skills.i_do_script: Every algebra expression is built from parts with names, and today we learn the names. Look at 5x + 8. It has two terms, separated by the plus sign: 5x and 8. In the term 5x, the letter x is the variable and the 5 riding in front of it is the coefficient -- the number multiplying the variable. The 8 has no variable at all, so it's the constant. I'm going to point at parts and you'll name them, like labeling the parts of a bike.

canonical_error.pattern: Confuses the coefficient with the constant -- names whichever number is most visible
canonical_error.example: For 6m + 5, student says the coefficient of m is 5 because 5 is 'the other number'
canonical_error.why: The student treats 'coefficient' and 'constant' as interchangeable words for 'a number in the expression.' They haven't anchored coefficient to its job: the number MULTIPLYING the variable, physically attached to it.

redirect_script.stop: Which number is actually touching the variable?
redirect_script.prompt: Circle the term that contains the variable. The coefficient lives INSIDE that circle, glued to the letter. The constant is the loner term with no letter at all. Now which is which?
redirect_script.praise: You anchored each name to its job -- coefficient multiplies, constant stands alone.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 7x + 4
How many pieces do you see in 7x + 4, and what symbol separates them?
Right -- the plus sign splits it into two terms: 7x and 4. Draw a box around each term.
Look inside the first box, 7x. Which symbol is the variable, and what is the 7 doing to it?
The 7 is multiplying the x -- that's why we call it the coefficient. Coefficient means 'the multiplier glued to the letter.'
Now look at the second box, 4. Does it have a variable? So what do we call a term that's just a number sitting alone?

If the student names 4 as the coefficient of x, they grabbed the loner number. Ask: 'Is the 4 touching the x? Circle the term with the variable -- the coefficient lives inside that circle. So which number multiplies x?'
So in 7x + 4 the coefficient of x is 7, and the 4 is the constant. Coefficient multiplies the variable; the constant stands alone.

skills.name: Combine like terms to write equivalent expressions
skills.i_do_script: Like terms are terms that count the same thing. In 6r + 6 + r + 2 + 2r, the r-terms count r's and the plain numbers count ones -- so they live in separate piles. Watch me sort: 6r + r + 2r is 9r (remember, r alone is 1r), and 6 + 2 is 8. The whole thing becomes 9r + 8. Same value, shorter name. The one rule: r's only combine with r's, and numbers only combine with numbers.

canonical_error.pattern: Merges unlike terms -- adds constants into coefficients as if every number were the same kind
canonical_error.example: Simplifies 4x + 5 + 2x as 11x, adding the 4, 5, and 2 together
canonical_error.why: The student sees three numbers and adds them all, ignoring what each number counts. 4x counts x's and 5 counts ones -- different units, like adding 4 dogs + 5 cats and calling it 11 dogs.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on -- do all of those terms count the same thing?
redirect_script.prompt: Underline every term that has the variable, and circle every plain number. Only the underlined ones can combine with each other, and only the circled ones can combine with each other. Now re-add each pile.
redirect_script.praise: You sorted before you added -- that's exactly what combining like terms means.

skills.name: Apply commutative and associative properties to write equivalent expressions
skills.i_do_script: When we combined like terms, we quietly rearranged the expression first -- and today we name the rules that make that legal. The commutative property says order doesn't matter for addition: 9 + 6n and 6n + 9 name the same number. The associative property says grouping doesn't matter for addition: (4y + 6y) + y and 4y + (6y + y) are the same. But here's the catch -- these rules are ONLY for addition and multiplication. 15 - b is NOT the same as b - 15, and we can prove it by plugging in a number.

canonical_error.pattern: Applies the commutative property to subtraction or division -- believes 'order never matters'
canonical_error.example: Student claims 15 - b is equivalent to b - 15 'by the commutative property'
canonical_error.why: The student learned 'you can switch the order' as a universal rule instead of a property OF addition and multiplication. They've never tested it on subtraction, where b = 5 gives 15 - 5 = 10 but 5 - 15 does not.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- does switching work for THAT operation?

vocabulary.definition: For addition and multiplication, the order can switch without changing the value: a + b = b + a.
For addition and multiplication, the grouping (parentheses) can move without changing the value: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c).

Two expressions that name the same number for every value of the variable.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 9 + 6n     6n + 9
Do these two expressions name the same number? How could we find out without just trusting our eyes?
Let n = 2. What does each expression equal?
Both are 21. Switching the order of an ADDITION never changes the value -- that's the commutative property. 'Commute' means to move back and forth, like commuting to school.
Now write: 15 - b     b - 15
A student says these are equivalent by the commutative property. Let b = 5 -- what does each side give you?

Students should get 10 for 15 - 5 and see that 5 - 15 can't also be 10. If someone insists they're equal, have them act it out: having 15 dollars and spending 5 is not the same as having 5 and spending 15.
So the commutative property has a boundary: addition and multiplication only. Never subtraction, never division. When in doubt, test a value -- the numbers always tell the truth.

skills.name: Justify whether two expressions are equivalent using substitution
skills.i_do_script: Two expressions are equivalent when they name the same number no matter what value the variable takes. So substitution is our lie detector. A student claims 3.5(x + 6) equals 3.5x + 21. Let's test x = 2: the left side is 3.5 times 8, which is 28, and the right side is 7 plus 21, which is 28. Same number -- the claim survives. But if even ONE value gives two different numbers, the expressions are not equivalent, case closed. Looks can lie; substitution can't.

canonical_error.why: The student thinks equivalent means 'made of the same ingredients' rather than 'names the same number for every value.' They've never operationalized the definition, so a near-miss like 2x + 3 looks identical to the real expansion 2x + 6.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 'A student says 3.5(x + 6) = 3.5x + 21. Use x = 2 to decide if the student is correct.'
Before any math: what does 'equivalent' actually promise? Equal for which values?
Equal for EVERY value. So we test one and see if the claim survives. Substitution is our lie detector.
Left side: 3.5(2 + 6) = 3.5 x 8 = 28. Write each step.
Now you do the right side: 3.5 x 2 + 21. Work it all the way to one number.
Watch that students evaluate 3.5 x 2 as 7 before adding 21 -- multiply before add. If someone adds 2 + 21 first, ask which operation goes first.
28 and 28. What's our verdict -- and how would the verdict change if we'd gotten 28 and 25?
One mismatch would sink the claim forever -- that's a counterexample. Matching values support the claim, and the distributive property tells us it holds for every x, not just 2.

practice_problems.stem: Evaluate 2x + 6 when x = 4.
Evaluate 2(x + 3) when x = 4.
practice_problems.notes: Pairing with the previous warm-up quietly plants the equivalence.

practice_problems.stem: Test y = 3: are 4(y + 2) and 4y + 8 equivalent? Show both computations.
Leo decided whether two expressions are equivalent. Find the flaw in his justification and fix it.
shown_work: Leo writes: Yes -- both have a 3, an x, and a 4,
so they are the same expression.
practice_problems.answer: Leo never substituted a value. Test x = 2: 3(2 + 4) = 18 but 3(2) + 4 = 10. Not equivalent -- 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12. Same ingredients does not mean same value.
practice_problems.notes: The judging-by-appearance error -- the fix is running the test.

practice_problems.stem: Show that 5x + 5 and 5(x + 1) are equivalent using x = 6.
Ben tests x = 1 and finds 2x + 4 = 6 and 6x = 6, so he says they are equivalent. Test x = 3 and give the verdict.
practice_problems.answer: Not equivalent. At x = 3: 2(3) + 4 = 10 but 6(3) = 18. One matching value was a coincidence -- equivalence must hold for every value.
practice_problems.notes: The one-lucky-value trap; x = 1 makes many non-equivalent pairs collide.

practice_problems.stem: Find a value of x where 5x + 3 and 8x give the SAME number, then explain why the two expressions are still not equivalent.
practice_problems.answer: x = 1 (both give 8). They are not equivalent because equivalence requires equal values for EVERY x -- and x = 2 gives 13 vs 16.
practice_problems.notes: Reverses direction: produce the coincidence, then reject it.

practice_problems.stem: Write an expression equivalent to 4(2x + 3), then prove your claim with x = 5.
practice_problems.notes: Create-and-justify -- the standard's two verbs in one item.

activities.title: Truly Equivalent or Impostor?
materials: 8 expression cards and 10 partner cards (two impostors)
activities.instructions:
1. Spread all cards face up.
2. Partners match each left-column expression to its truly equivalent partner -- but two partner cards are impostors that match nothing.
3. NO match may be declared until the pair proves it: substitute x = 2 (or the variable's value of your choice) into both cards and show equal results.
4. Impostors must be convicted with a counterexample, written down.
5. Debrief: what made the impostors so convincing before you tested them?

activities.title: Leo's Look-Alike Trap
activities.instructions:
1. Students read Leo's claim that 3(x + 4) and 3x + 4 are equivalent 'because both have a 3, an x, and a 4.'
2. They name what's missing from his justification (no substitution -- no evidence) and run the test themselves with x = 2.
3. They write the verdict as a full sentence: 'Not equivalent, because when x = 2 the expressions give ___ and ___.'
4. Share out: can an equivalence claim EVER be justified just by how the expressions look?

content.worked_problem: Are 3(x + 4) and 3x + 4 equivalent? Leo says yes -- both have a 3, an x, and a 4.
content.error_step: Leo judged by ingredients instead of substituting a value.
content.why: Equivalent means equal for every value. Testing x = 2: 3(6) = 18 but 6 + 4 = 10 -- a counterexample, so not equivalent. The real expansion is 3x + 12.

activities.title: Lie Detector
materials: Claim cards (an equation that may be true or false)
activities.instructions:
1. Flip a claim card, e.g. '4(x + 2) = 4x + 8' or '3(n + 5) = 3n + 5.'
2. Roll the die -- the roll is your test value. Everyone substitutes it into both sides on their whiteboard.
3. Boards up: EQUAL or UNEQUAL? Unequal convicts the claim as a lie; the group states the counterexample out loud.
4. If equal, roll once more and re-test before declaring the claim 'survives.'
5. Debrief: why does one UNEQUAL end the game for a claim, while two EQUALs still don't fully prove it?

strategy_links.why: Substitution testing IS a number talk: pick a value, compute both ways, and let the numbers arbitrate the claim.
Partners must convince each other with computed evidence -- Think-Pair-Share makes the justification verbal before it's written.
Thinking aloud through 'equivalent means equal for EVERY value, so I'll test one' models the justification structure itself.

questioning_prompts: What does 'equivalent' promise -- equal for which values?
You tested one value and they matched. Are you done? What would make you MORE sure?
You tested one value and they DIDN'T match. Are you done? Why is one mismatch enough?
Why is x = 1 a risky test value for a claim like 5x + 3 = 8x?
Which property explains WHY these two will match for every value, not just yours?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student declares two expressions equivalent 'because they have the same numbers and letters' without computing anything.
misconception_redirects.say: Pick a value like x = 4 and substitute it into BOTH expressions separately. Work each one all the way to a single number. Do the two numbers match?
misconception_redirects.praise: You let the numbers decide instead of the way it looks -- that's a real justification.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student tests one value (often x = 1 or x = 0), gets a match by coincidence, and declares equivalence -- e.g., 5x + 3 and 8x at x = 1.
misconception_redirects.say: One match supports the claim but doesn't seal it -- try x = 2 as a second witness. Do they still match? A property (like distribution) is what proves it for EVERY value.
misconception_redirects.praise: Good instinct getting a second witness -- coincidence values can't survive two tests.

quick_checks.prompt: Are 2(x + 5) and 2x + 5 equivalent? You have 30 seconds -- justify with a number.
quick_checks.look_for: Not equivalent, with a test like x = 3 giving 16 vs 11. Saying 'yes, they look the same' means the appearance-based misconception is live; no test value at all means the justification habit isn't built.

quick_checks.prompt: Your partner tested x = 0 on 7x + 4 and 4 + 7x and got 4 both times. What CAN'T x = 0 tell you here, and what value would you add?
quick_checks.look_for: x = 0 wipes out the x-terms, so it can't distinguish the coefficients; add any nonzero value. Students who see nothing wrong with 0 don't yet see how a test value can be blind to part of the expression.

worked_solution.stem: A student says 3.5(x + 6) = 3.5x + 21. Substitute x = 2 into both expressions to decide if the student is correct.

steps.annotation: Substitute 2 for x, finish the parentheses first, then multiply.
Substitute into the OTHER expression separately -- multiply before adding.

steps.math: 28 = 28  -->  the student is correct; the expressions are equal at x = 2
steps.annotation: Matching values support the claim -- and the distributive property (3.5 x 6 = 21) guarantees it for every x, not just 2.

faded_example.stem: Are 2(4x + 1) and 8x + 1 equivalent? Test x = 3 and justify your answer.
faded_example.answer: Not equivalent -- at x = 3 they give 26 and 25.

steps.annotation: Substitute 3 for x and work the parentheses first.
Substitute x = 3 into the second expression and work it to one number.
Compare the two numbers and write the verdict: equivalent or not, because the values are equal or unequal.

sentence_starters: The expressions are ___ because when x = ___, they equal ___ and ___.
One counterexample is enough because equivalent means equal for ___ value.

skills.name: Combine properties to simplify and write multiple equivalent expressions
skills.i_do_script: Now we chain the properties together. Take 2(3x + 4) + 5x + 1. First the distributive property clears the parentheses: 6x + 8. Now the expression is 6x + 8 + 5x + 1, and the commutative property lets me regroup: 6x + 5x is 11x, and 8 + 1 is 9. Final answer: 11x + 9. The order matters -- distribute FIRST, then combine. The 5x outside the parentheses can't jump inside before the 2 has done its job.

canonical_error.pattern: Pulls outside terms into the parentheses before distributing -- combines across the grouping
canonical_error.why: The student treats the parentheses as decoration, so 4x looks like just another term to gather. But the parentheses mark what the 3 multiplies -- moving 4x inside makes the 3 multiply it too, tripling a term that was never supposed to be tripled.

redirect_script.stop: Freeze -- has the multiplier done its job yet?
redirect_script.prompt: The parentheses are a locked room: only what's inside gets multiplied. Distribute first and write the expression with no parentheses at all. THEN gather your like terms.
redirect_script.praise: Distribute, then combine -- you ran the properties in the right order.

skills.item_template: A multi-step expression like a(bx + c) + dx + e is given to simplify completely, or the student writes two or more expressions equivalent to a given one (e.g., 9(7x + 8)) using any properties. NR response, one unique variable in distributive parts, whole numbers.

sample_items.stem:
Simplify the expression completely.

  2(3x + 4) + 5x + 1
sample_items.distractor_logic: 18x + 3-style answers pull the 5x inside before distributing; 11x + 5 distributes partially (2 x 4 skipped); 20x merges constants into the coefficient

sample_items.stem:
Simplify the expression completely.

  4(2n + 3) + 6
sample_items.distractor_logic: 8n + 9 partially distributes then adds; 8n + 3 + 6 = 8n + 9 same trap; 4(2n + 9) = 8n + 36 pulls the 6 inside first

sample_items.stem: Write two different expressions that are equivalent to 9(7x + 8).
sample_items.distractor_logic: 63x + 8 partially distributes; 16x + 17-style answers add instead of multiplying

sample_items.stem:
An expression is given.

  3(2m + m + 3m)

Write the equivalent simplified expression.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 15m combines to 5m inside (missing the lone m's invisible 1) then multiplies; 6m + m + 3m = 10m distributes to the first term only; 14m + 9m mixes both errors

sample_items.stem:
Simplify the expression completely.

  5(2y + 1) + 3y + 4
sample_items.distractor_logic: 5(2y + 1 + 3y) = 25y + 5 pulls the 3y inside first; 13y + 5 skips the 5 x 1 or drops the + 4

vocabulary.definition: Keep applying properties until no parentheses remain and no like terms are left uncombined.
The multiplier outside the parentheses multiplies every term inside -- do this FIRST.
Terms counting the same thing -- combine them only after the parentheses are gone.
Different-looking expressions that name the same number for every value -- one expression can have many equivalent forms.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for 7.AF.1 -- linear expressions with rational coefficients.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 2(3x + 4) + 5x + 1
There are two jobs here -- distributing and combining like terms. Which has to happen first, and what decides that?
The parentheses are a locked room: the 2 multiplies ONLY what's inside. The 5x and the 1 are outside the room, so they wait.
Distribute the 2 -- both arrows. What does 2(3x + 4) become?
Rewrite the whole expression with no parentheses: 6x + 8 + 5x + 1.
Now which property lets us reorder and regroup these four terms? Gather the piles: what are the x-terms, and what are the constants?
If a student had wanted to write 2(3x + 4 + 5x) at the start, test it now: x = 1 gives the original 2(7) + 5 + 1 = 20, but 2(3 + 4 + 5) = 24. The locked room matters.
6x + 5x is 11x, and 8 + 1 is 9. So 2(3x + 4) + 5x + 1 = 11x + 9. Distribute first, then commute and combine -- three properties, one clean chain.

practice_problems.stem: Expand: 3(2x + 1)
Simplify: 6n + 2n + 5
Simplify completely: 2(4x + 3) + 5x
Ryan simplified an expression. Find his mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: 10x + 3. The 4x lives OUTSIDE the parentheses, so the 3 never multiplies it. Distribute first: 6x + 3 + 4x, then combine: 10x + 3. Check x = 1: original 3(3) + 4 = 13 and 10 + 3 = 13, but Ryan's 18 + 3 = 21.
practice_problems.notes: The combine-across-the-parentheses error -- the locked-room fix.

practice_problems.stem: Simplify completely: 5(y + 2) + 2y + 3
Simplify completely: 4(3m + 2m)
practice_problems.notes: Two legal routes -- combine inside first (4 x 5m) or distribute first (12m + 8m). Both land on 20m; have students try both.

practice_problems.stem: Write THREE different expressions equivalent to 6(3x + 4).
practice_problems.notes: The above-proficiency demand: many names for one expression.

practice_problems.stem: Simplify completely: 2(x + 3) + 3(x + 1)
practice_problems.notes: Two distributions before any combining -- watch the order discipline hold up.

activities.title: Long Name, Short Name
materials: 8 multi-step expression cards and 10 simplified cards (two decoys)
activities.instructions:
1. Spread all cards face up: long unsimplified expressions on the left, short simplified ones on the right.
2. Partners match each long expression to its fully simplified form -- two short cards are decoys built from the classic errors.
3. Every match must be proven one of two ways: show the distribute-then-combine steps, or substitute x = 2 into both cards.
4. Convict each decoy: which error would produce it?
5. Debrief: both decoys came from doing the two jobs in the wrong order -- which job must always come first?

activities.title: Many Names Challenge
activities.instructions:
1. Post a target expression like 9(7x + 8). Set a 3-minute timer.
2. Each student writes as many DIFFERENT equivalent expressions as they can: expanded (63x + 72), reordered (9(8 + 7x)), refactored (3(21x + 24)), decomposed (63x + 70 + 2)...
3. Boards up. The group audits each claim -- any challenged expression gets the x = 1 substitution test.
4. One point per surviving expression; the round's most creative legal form earns a bonus point.
5. Debrief: which property produced each of your names?

activities.title: The Locked Room
activities.instructions:
1. Students read Ryan's work: he pulled 4x inside the parentheses before distributing.
2. They draw a box around the parentheses (the locked room), mark which term Ryan smuggled in, and write the correct simplification.
3. They prove the verdict by substituting x = 1 into the original, their answer, and Ryan's.
4. Share out: what does the multiplier do to anything that sneaks inside the room?

content.error_step: Ryan moved the outside term 4x into the parentheses before distributing.
content.why: The parentheses mark exactly what the 3 multiplies. Smuggling 4x inside makes the 3 triple it. Correct chain: distribute (6x + 3 + 4x), then combine (10x + 3). Check x = 1: original 13, correct 13, Ryan's 21.

strategy_links.why: Multi-step chains need gradual release: model the distribute-then-combine order, run one together, then release.
A correct chain next to Ryan's smuggled-term chain isolates the one move that differs -- the order of the two jobs.
Whiteboard Pass on a single multi-step problem shows exactly which step -- distributing or combining -- each student breaks on.

questioning_prompts: Two jobs live in this expression -- distributing and combining. Which goes first, and why?
Which terms are inside the locked room, and which are waiting outside?
After you distribute, read your new expression -- are there any parentheses left? Any like terms left?
You wrote three equivalent forms -- which property produced each one?
How could you check your simplified answer in under a minute?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student gathers an outside term into the parentheses before distributing -- turns 3(2x + 1) + 4x into 3(6x + 1).
misconception_redirects.say: The parentheses are a locked room: only what's inside gets multiplied. Distribute first and write the expression with no parentheses at all. THEN gather your like terms.
misconception_redirects.praise: Distribute, then combine -- you ran the properties in the right order.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student distributes to the first term only in the multi-step setting -- 2(3x + 4) + 5x becomes 6x + 4 + 5x.
misconception_redirects.say: Two terms inside means two arrows -- the 2 owes the 4 a multiplication too. Redo just the distribution step, then bring the 5x back in.
misconception_redirects.praise: Both arrows first, outside terms after -- that's the full chain.

quick_checks.prompt: Simplify 2(n + 3) + 4n, narrating each property as you use it.
quick_checks.look_for: Distributive (2n + 6), then commutative/combining (6n + 6). An answer of 2(5n + 3) = 10n + 6 means the outside 4n got smuggled inside -- rerun the locked-room routine.

quick_checks.prompt: Give me TWO expressions equivalent to 8(2x + 3), each made with a different property.
quick_checks.look_for: E.g. 16x + 24 (distributive) and 8(3 + 2x) (commutative) or 4(4x + 6) (refactoring). Only producing the expansion suggests the student has one tool, not a toolbox.

steps.annotation: The parentheses go first. The 2 multiplies both inside terms -- the 5x and 1 wait outside.
No parentheses left. Now the commutative property lets us gather like terms.
Combine each pile separately -- x's with x's, ones with ones.
Check with x = 1: original is 2(7) + 5 + 1 = 20, and 11(1) + 9 = 20. Equivalent.
Clear the parentheses first -- both arrows. The 3y and 4 wait outside.
Rewrite the whole expression with no parentheses.
Gather the piles: add the y-terms, then add the constants.
Write the simplified expression, then check it with y = 1.

sentence_starters: I distributed first because the ___ only multiplies what is ___ the parentheses.
My three equivalent forms used the ___, ___, and ___ properties.

foundation.label: Foundation
foundation.description: Tier III -- 2+ grade levels below. If a student can't access Looking Back, start here.

looking_back.label: Looking Back
looking_back.description: Prerequisite skills -- fix these first if a student can't access grade-level work

looking_forward.label: Looking Forward
looking_forward.description: Extension skills -- for students ready to push ahead

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S4 (distributive property) -- the heart of the standard. If they pass, move to S5 (justify by substitution) and S6 (combine properties). If they fail, check whether the gap is S1 (naming the parts) or S2 (combining like terms). S3 (commutative/associative) is the branch skill: probe it when a student can combine like terms but can't say why the rearranging is legal.
